elements.text: A node links hubs into one network, even when they are far apart. It does not move anything itself, it only connects: items and fluids then travel between the hubs in that network.

The node window shows its links as a list and on a map around it, north up. The order of the list sets the priority; drag a row by the handle on its right to change it. The Highlight button shows the selected block in the world.
A hub goes next to a chest or a machine. You set each of its six sides separately: take, give, both or nothing.

You can choose which items go through, how many to keep in the neighbouring chest, and whether to hand them out in turns. A hub moves things both to its neighbours and across the whole linked network.
The hub window lists all six sides on the left and the settings of the selected one on the right: mode, input or output filter, toggles and the upgrade slot. Right-click a side to cycle its mode.
Use it to link devices. Click a node, then a hub or machine, and they end up in the same network. The magnet's remote controller is bound the same way.
It also links drill beacons to the industrial miner.

The simplest automation, no hubs needed. Put one into a machine's upgrade slot: a **pusher** sends finished items into the chest next to it, a **puller** takes what the machine needs from the neighbouring chest. Items and fluids each have their own.
They go on a side of a hub. A hub with an upgrade moves things more often and more at a time. There are three tiers, and the third is the fastest.

They go into a machine's slots. The **accelerator** makes the machine work faster, but it uses more power. There are three accelerators, and several of them stack. **Parallel modules** let it make several items at once: 8, 32 or 64.
The blast furnace, the cultivator and logistics have their own upgrades, described in their entries.
**Crates** hold items: 54, 72 or 90 slots. **Barrels** hold fluids: 32, 128 or 512 buckets, and they keep their fluid even when broken. Each tier is made from the one before.
They are cheap and connect easily to hubs and machines.
